title: Myoelectric pattern recognition with augmented reality relieves 48-year phantom limb pain in a treatment-resistant amputee
summary: A 72-year-old with 48 years of intractable phantom limb pain reached pain-free periods after ML-driven phantom motor execution.
account: A 72-year-old man's below-elbow amputation in 1965 left him with 48 years of phantom limb pain, resistant to mirror therapy, drugs, acupuncture and hypnosis. He was treated by a Chalmers University of Technology / Sahlgrenska University Hospital team (both in Gothenburg; the paper does not name the treatment site). Treatment ran for 18 weeks from March 2013. The exact start date is not reported. Stump surface electromyography was classified by myoelectric pattern recognition (linear discriminant analysis and a multilayer perceptron in the open-source BioPatRec platform). It drove a virtual limb shown in augmented reality and a racing game. After four weeks he reported episodes of lower pain intensity, after ten weeks near-absent pain developing into completely pain-free periods. His phantom fist relaxed and he could move the phantom freely (Frontiers in Neuroscience, 2014).
purpose: Treat phantom limb pain by letting the patient execute phantom movements decoded from stump muscle activity
system: Phantom motor execution: BioPatRec myoelectric pattern recognition (LDA and MLP classifiers) driving augmented/virtual reality and a racing game
model_version: BioPatRec, LDA one-vs-one and MLP per degree of freedom
developer: Chalmers University of Technology, Biomedical Engineering Division (academic lab; study part-funded by Integrum AB)
deployer: Chalmers University of Technology and Sahlgrenska University Hospital, Gothenburg (inferred from author affiliations; the paper does not name the treatment site)
segment: Upper-limb amputees with phantom limb pain

ratings.reason: An identifiable patient with 48 years of treatment-resistant pain reached pain-free periods and regained phantom movement. The case gives no long-term follow-up, so a durable life-changing effect is not established.
Single case. The same group later ran a 14-patient trial. No population effect is documented.

ai_role.statement: The pattern-recognition classifiers turn stump EMG into predicted phantom movements that the virtual limb executes. The authors argue that this engagement of motor circuitry, rather than a mirror of the contralateral limb, is the therapeutic mechanism. So the AI component is central, though the single-case design cannot isolate it.

headline: BioPatRec pattern recognition eases 48-year phantom limb pain
metric: after ten weeks near-absent pain developing into completely pain-free periods

comparator.against: the patient's pain after 48 years of conventional treatments (mirror therapy, drugs, acupuncture, hypnosis)
comparator.before: constant burning pain of an intensity of 3 on a scale from 0 to 10 (SF-MGPQ)
comparator.after: gradually reduced to complete pain-free periods
comparator.quote: The sustained level of pain reported by the patient was gradually reduced to complete pain-free periods.

later.note: A single-group trial of 14 patients at four clinics in Sweden and Slovenia reported significant reductions in phantom limb pain that held at six-month follow-up.
later.quote: Between Sept 15, 2014, and April 10, 2015, 14 patients with intractable chronic phantom limb pain, for whom conventional treatments failed, were enrolled.
